lines.text: Edinburgh made me look up. I still wonder what a place can reveal when you give it a moment.
This rented flat became our base, and the chair looked like a good place to land.
I liked having a quiet room to return to after the city had filled my head.
There’s something useful about arriving before you have a plan for every hour.
I could take a breath here, then step back out and see what caught my attention.
The ordinary things in a room can make it feel like yours, at least for a while.
On the Royal Mile, we stopped outside Old Town Chambers and shared the street for a moment.
The hotel sits at 329 High Street; the Royal Mile runs about a Scots mile between the Castle and Holyroodhouse.
I remember the flowers, the doorway, and how nice it was not to hurry past each other.
Then we crossed into St Giles’. It felt natural to stop talking and look up.
The church was founded by King David the First in 1124, though standing here feels very much about now.
The crown steeple probably dates from around 1500; even its exact date remains uncertain.
The east window drew me in, with paintings gathered below it and so much color overhead.
This great east window shows the Crucifixion and Ascension; a guide credits its glass to Ballantine of Edinburgh.
The inscription dates mark Falshaw’s Lord Provost term, from 1874 to 1877.
I couldn’t confidently identify every painting from where I stood, so I let the details stay open.
The church hosted John Bellany’s 1965 painting The Box Meeting in 2025; I’m not sure this is it.
Bellany grew up in Port Seton, where fishing life shaped his recurring boats, fishermen, and harbours.
By the Thames in London, I found myself looking across the water instead of checking the time.
That tower is 20 Fenchurch Street, known as the Walkie-Talkie, completed in 2014 at 155 metres.
Its upper floors hold the public Sky Garden, though from here I’m taking in the river and lights.
The trip ends in London, but the feeling I’m taking home is simpler: there’s always more to notice.
